unresolvedReleaseQuestions.question: Venue on a multi-county conviction petition. The controlling review states that S.B. 562 (2020) allows a person seeking expungement of convictions in more than one county to file in his or her county of residence. Section 61-11-26 was read in full at source on 2026-08-06 and the current text does not contain a residence-county venue option: subsections (a)(1) and (a)(2) both say 'petition the circuit court in which the conviction or convictions occurred', the subsection (d) proviso requires a multiple-misdemeanour petition to 'identify and group such information by circuit court, as applicable', and § 61-11-26a(a) says 'may petition the circuit court or circuit courts in which the conviction or convictions occurred'. Read together the current text supports one petition covering several counties, grouped by circuit court and served on the prosecuting attorney of each county of conviction, but it does not name a residence-county forum. Venue for the single-county case is unaffected and unambiguous. Until counsel resolves this, the packet directs a multi-county participant to the circuit court of conviction and adds a local-check instruction rather than promising a residence-county filing.

Whether relief under § 60A-4-407 or § 17C-5-2b counts against the once-per-lifetime limit in § 61-11-26. Section 61-11-26(o) by its terms reaches only §§ 61-11-26 and 61-11-26a, and neither § 60A-4-407 nor § 17C-5-2b cross-references it; both were read in full at source on 2026-08-06 and neither contains a limit referring to § 61-11-26. The textual reading is therefore that they are separate limits in separate statutes, but a participant deciding whether to spend their one lifetime petition needs a settled answer rather than a textual inference.

Whether the $200 circuit clerk civil filing fee under § 59-1-11(a)(1) is in practice charged in full on an expungement petition in every circuit, and whether any circuit applies an indigency waiver. The statutory amount and its statutory basis are now settled at source; the practice, and whether the ordinary civil indigency affidavit is accepted, is not.

How far the § 17C-5-2(j)(1) expungement reaches. The subsection expunges 'the person's record as it relates to the alleged offense' and names no agency, in contrast to §§ 61-11-25 and 61-11-26, which expressly reach agency and law-enforcement records and impose a 60-day certification duty. Whether the State Police record and the arresting agency's record are cleared, or only the court record, is not established, and it changes what the participant should be told to expect on a background check.

What a participant does if the programme was completed but the court has not in fact dismissed and expunged. Section 17C-5-2(j)(1) was read in full at source on 2026-08-06 and imposes the duty on the court in mandatory terms — 'the court shall dismiss the charge against the person and expunge the person's record as it relates to the alleged offense' — but describes no application, no motion to enforce and no remedy if the court does not act. Whether a motion to enforce lies, and whether LegalEase may generate one, is unresolved. Until it is, the guidance directs the participant to the clerk and, failing that, to a lawyer, and no enforcement pleading is generated.
